title: Meter and form
period: English poetry, sixteenth to nineteenth centuries

sources.title: Two soliloquies from Hamlet
sources.author: William Shakespeare
sources.citation: William Shakespeare, The Tragedy of Hamlet, Prince of Denmark (c. 1600–1601), Act II, scene 2, and Act III, scene 1, in The Complete Works of William Shakespeare, edited by W. J. Craig (London: Oxford University Press, 1914). Project Gutenberg eBook 1524.
sources.context: Hamlet's soliloquies are in unrhymed iambic pentameter, the blank verse Shakespeare's company made the standard medium of the public stage. Both passages show the meter bending under the pressure of thought, from regular beats to short broken lines.
questions: Where in these speeches does the meter run most regularly, and where does it break or pause?
Hamlet ends one line 'To die—to sleep' and another 'For Hecuba?' What do these short lines do to the rhythm?
Count the stresses in 'To be, or not to be, that is the question.' Does the line end on a stress?

sources.title: Break, Break, Break and The Charge of the Light Brigade
sources.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
sources.citation: Alfred, Lord Tennyson, 'Break, Break, Break' (1842), in The Early Poems of Alfred Lord Tennyson, edited by John Churton Collins (London: Methuen, 1900); and 'The Charge of the Light Brigade' (1854; revised 1855), in Maud, and Other Poems (London: Edward Moxon, 1855). Project Gutenberg eBooks 8601 and 56913.
sources.context: Tennyson wrote 'The Charge of the Light Brigade' within weeks of the disastrous cavalry charge at Balaclava in 1854. Its falling rhythm, short lines, and refrain are usually heard as the beat of horses and the headlong rush of the brigade.
questions: Read the opening of 'The Charge of the Light Brigade' aloud. Where do the stresses fall, and what does the pattern suggest?
Which words rhyme, and where does a rhyme fall inside a line rather than at its end?
What does the refrain 'Rode the six hundred' do each time it returns?

sources.title: Song of Myself, sections 1–2
sources.author: Walt Whitman
sources.citation: Walt Whitman, Leaves of Grass (Boston: Small, Maynard & Co., 1899), 'Song of Myself,' sections 1–2. Project Gutenberg eBook 1322.
sources.context: Whitman's long unrhymed lines broke with the metrical forms of the English tradition. Their rhythm comes from breath, repetition, and the sweep of the sentence rather than from a repeating foot.
questions: How does Whitman divide these lines, and what seems to determine where each one ends?
Find a phrase that repeats. What does the repetition do to the rhythm?
Try to scan one of these lines as iambic pentameter. Why does the attempt fail?

interpretations.claim: Fussell argued that meter is not a container for meaning but part of it: because a reader expects a metrical pattern, a poet can make meaning by fulfilling, delaying, or breaking that expectation, and the substitutions that vary a line are expressive choices rather than noise.
interpretations.note: Attridge and other beat theorists reply that the foot-and-substitution vocabulary Fussell uses is a misleading import from Greek, and that English rhythm is better described by beats; the dispute is whether a substitution is an event in the poem or only in its description.

interpretations.claim: Attridge argued that the traditional foot-and-substitution model misdescribes English verse. Rhythm, on his account, rests on the alternation of beats and offbeats in a stress-timed language, so a line should be described as a sequence of beats rather than a string of Greek feet.
interpretations.note: Traditional prosodists, and generative metricists such as Morris Halle and Samuel Jay Keyser, defend the foot as a useful abstraction and argue that beat theory under-describes the syllable; the disagreement is partly about what a description of verse is for.

activities.prompt: In English verse, what is a 'foot'?
choices: A repeated unit of stressed and unstressed syllables
A line of exactly ten syllables
A pause at the end of a line
A rhyme between two lines
activities.feedback: A foot is the small repeated unit of meter — an iamb, trochee, anapest, dactyl, or spondee.

activities.prompt: Which foot is an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one?
choices: Iamb
Trochee
Dactyl
Spondee
activities.feedback: An iamb rises from weak to strong: 'to be,' 'the sun,' 'again.'

activities.prompt: 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?' is written in which meter?
choices: Iambic pentameter
Trochaic tetrameter
Anapestic tetrameter
Dactylic hexameter
activities.feedback: Five iambs: shall I | compare | thee to | a sum- | mer's day.

activities.prompt: What does the falling, galloping rhythm of 'The Charge of the Light Brigade' mainly suggest?
choices: The headlong ride of the cavalry
A calm sea voyage
A slow funeral procession
A quiet country walk
activities.feedback: The dactyls, anapests, and short refrain lines imitate the horses' gallop and the rush into the valley.

choices: A rhyme that matches some but not all of the sound
A rhyme at the start of two lines
A rhyme in a foreign language
A rhyme that repeats the same word
activities.feedback: Slant or near rhyme is imperfect: Dickinson's 'soul'/'all' and Owen's pararhymes are examples.

activities.prompt: What distinguishes blank verse from free verse?
choices: Blank verse is unrhymed iambic pentameter; free verse has no fixed meter
Blank verse rhymes; free verse does not
Blank verse has no meter; free verse is metrical
They are two names for the same form
activities.feedback: Blank verse keeps the iambic pentameter line but drops rhyme; free verse abandons the fixed metrical pattern as well.

choices: Runs the sense past the line break
Ends the sense at the line break
Adds an extra stress to the line
Repeats the line as a refrain
activities.feedback: Enjambment sets the metrical pause and the syntactic pause in different places, as Milton often does.

activities.prompt: In Marlowe's 'Come live with me and be my love, / And we will all the pleasures prove,' the pair 'love'/'prove' is an example of…
choices: Eye rhyme
Perfect rhyme
Internal rhyme
Feminine rhyme
activities.feedback: The words look alike but no longer sound alike — an eye rhyme, a fossil of a change in pronunciation.

activities.prompt: How does the English or Shakespearean sonnet arrange its fourteen lines?
choices: Three quatrains and a closing couplet
An octave and a sestet
Twelve lines and a two-line refrain
Seven rhymed couplets
activities.feedback: The English sonnet rhymes abab cdcd efef gg; the Petrarchan form instead divides into an octave and a sestet.

activities.prompt: Compare how meter works in Hamlet's 'To be, or not to be' soliloquy and in Whitman's 'Song of Myself.' What does each poet use to organize the line, and what does that organization let each passage do?
activities.context: Shakespeare: 'To be, or not to be, that is the question: / Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer' — Whitman: 'I celebrate myself, and sing myself, / And what I assume you shall assume, / For every atom belonging to me as good belongs to you.'
rubric: names a device or pattern in each (for example, iambic pentameter and the line break or repetition)
uses a specific phrase from each passage
